prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which the magic-wavelength trap allows many atoms to be interrogated at once and has taken atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B019, to Katori and Ye. As Chair I put the question in the summary of what is discovered beyond better numbers, so here is my answer as an experimentalist. The magic-wavelength condition is a physical result, not a tuning exercise. It shows that an optical trap can hold neutral atoms so that the light shift cancels for the clock transition, which removes the old trade-off between long interrogation time and perturbation by the apparatus. That opened a regime that did not exist before: thousands of atoms, Hz-level lines, and systematic budgets near 1e-18, where a millimetre of height is visible as a gravitational redshift and where many-body and collisional effects in the lattice become measurement physics in themselves. Single-ion clocks and the comb prize of 2005 did not give that regime. The result is also reproduced and cross-checked at JILA, RIKEN, SYRTE, PTB and NIST with agreed budgets, which is the test I apply to any instrument-led claim, and it has already left the clock community, in geodesy, in bounds on drifting constants and in dark-matter searches. The citation should rest on the instrument and its physics. The redefinition of the second is a prospective consequence and should stay out of the citation and out of the rationale. Five of eight members already name the same two laureates, and nobody has proposed a different pair.
statement.case_against: The objection that I take most seriously, and which Eriksson, Mehlig and the caveats in my own colleagues' statements all point at, is that the committee would be honouring a fourth prize in one line (laser cooling 1997, comb 2005, ion control 2012, 2018 laser tools) and that a precision threshold is not the same as a discrete discovery. I think the magic-wavelength concept answers this, but it is a judgement and I do not claim it is beyond argument. The priority record for the first strontium lattice clock (Katori, JILA, SYRTE) has not been checked against documents by any of us, and I cannot rule out that Lemonde or Derevianko has a claim that a two-name prize would hide. If outside experts told us that the idea was already implicit in earlier proposals, or that the credit is split differently, I would reconsider. I also recognise that B019 gained support partly through colleagues moving to it after round 1, so the count should not carry weight in my judgement.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators (B012) because the interpretation is stable after more than fifteen years, and he notes that a prize on a new state of matter in a solid would balance the 2025 circuits prize. He also admits the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap and the 2016 overlap.
responses.response: I agree that stability of interpretation is the right test, and the quantum spin Hall state passes it. The clocks pass it too: the budgets are agreed across five laboratories and nobody disputes the numbers. My difficulty with B012 is attribution, which you state yourself. The HgTe route came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, Zhang has died, and a three-name set cannot repair that without a citation narrowed to 2D quantum spin Hall. Narrowing then brings the overlap with 2016 closer, since the state is classified by topology. I would accept your argument that a condensed-matter signal is worth balancing, and I have kept B012 as an alternative for that reason, but I do not see a configuration of B012 that is cleaner than Katori and Ye.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked the clocks sixth and moved to magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, valuing the structure of a compact theory followed by an experiment at the predicted angle. His own stated weakness is the missing first authors, Cao and others, and the unsettled mechanism.
responses.response: The structure you value is real and it is the strongest argument for B047. The Bistritzer-MacDonald angle was predicted and then found, which is rare. I still weigh maturity differently: eight years, a pairing mechanism nobody can yet state, and twist-angle disorder that limits reproducibility from sample to sample. You asked in effect whether waiting is neutral. For the clocks I think it is not, since the discovery is already confirmed in several laboratories. For B047, waiting costs the committee little, because the field will tell us in a few years which of its results are lasting. On your sixth place for the clocks, I answered the overlap point above: the comb counts optical frequencies, while the lattice clock builds the reference out of the atoms themselves. That is a different invention.

responses.point: Olsson holds B047 first and answers the credit question by pointing to the clean dates for prediction (2011) and discovery (2018), with Bistritzer kept because the continuum model is joint work.
responses.response: I accept that the dates are clean and that Bistritzer belongs with MacDonald on the theory side. The chair's question to you remains open for me: naming Jarillo-Herrero alone on the experimental side, when Cao and Fatemi did the measurements, is a hard choice and it is not resolved by the date argument. I would not call it fatal, because prizes have rested on group leaders before, but it makes this configuration weaker than a two-name clock prize where both names are the people who built the instruments. If the committee takes B047, I think we should state the credit limit openly in the rationale. For this year I still place it second.

responses.point: Kroll keeps B019 first, wants a clean proposal-plus-realisation citation, and asks for a check of priority between Katori, JILA and SYRTE for the first strontium lattice clock.
responses.response: I agree with the citation form, and I have tried to follow it above: the magic-wavelength concept and its realisation at the 1e-18 level, with nothing about the second. I support your request for a priority check. Because I am not an atomic physicist, I would ask for an outside expert opinion on lattice-clock priority before the final ballot and I would not rely on our own recollection, which both you and Lindroth say you are working from. I would also take Katori's proposal to be the conceptual contribution, with the Ye group delivering the demonstration of what it can do, and I would not widen the prize to theory.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength trap as a discovery in its own right, distinct from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
The priority record for the first strontium lattice clock, and whether Lemonde or Derevianko has a claim that two names would hide.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene will look more or less mature once the pairing mechanism is better understood, and whether naming Jarillo-Herrero alone on the experimental side can be defended.
Whether B012 can be put forward in a way that settles the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap and the 2016 overlap.
I rely on colleagues for atomic and condensed-matter physics and on recollection, not a verified record, for dates and accuracy figures.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has changed since round 1. I have no known institutional, collaborative or personal link to Katori, Ye or any other shortlisted name, and my own work on PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur is in astroparticle detectors, not atomic clocks. I rely on colleagues with atomic, condensed-matter and quantum-information expertise, and as Chair I am running the process and not adjusting my judgement to the count of supporters. Johansson and Kroll have declared a link to B004, which is not in my configuration.
